title: Categorical "the model does not adapt to this defect" in abstract/intro/conclusion/§3.2/App B is stronger than the §5.3 hedge and than the evidence supports
quote: the model does not adapt to this defect
explanation: The abstract ("the model does not adapt to this defect"), the introduction ("the model does not learn to avoid it"; Contribution 1 "for that defect the model does not adapt"), §3.2, App B and the conclusion ("so the model does not learn to avoid it") all state the r_t result as a flat negative. §5.3(i), the only place the test is defined, says something weaker: "it rules out strong adaptation to this defect, not weak adaptation or adaptation to others", with "no interval on r_t". The data behind the result are thin, and the headline claims leave this out. (a) Three runs, all Run A on MATH-500: one at 10−5, which the paper itself says "changed the outputs little" (§1, §4.2, §4.4), so a flat r_t there is expected whether or not adaptation pressure exists; and two seeds at 5×10−4 with rounds R0–R2, where R0 is the untrained base, so each run has only two trained checkpoints. (b) There are no intervals and no trend test. A 15.5–18.4% band is about 3 points wide, which is not obviously narrower than the sampling noise of a share computed on a few hundred V′-accepted generations whose count also falls as accuracy falls. (c) The denominator (V′-accepted generations) changes with training: as accuracy falls the mix of solved problems shifts, and if compound-answer problems (where the defect bites) are lost at a different rate than others, a change in the mix can hide or fake a trend. The paper does not report r_t on a fixed problem set. (d) Under restart-from-base each round trains a fresh LoRA adapter for one epoch on a few hundred examples, so the room for cumulative adaptation is limited by design. That bears on whether a flat r_t says anything about GVT in general. (e) App B notes that r_t assumes V′ accepts no wrong answer, which was not measured. Given (a)–(e), the honest headline is the §5.3 wording: "no evidence of strong adaptation to this one defect in three runs". The abstract should use that wording, not "does not adapt". The abstract follows this with "Nor does it improve", which presents both branches of the research question as settled negatives. The introduction's own framing ("the pre-set rule is silent") and §5.1 ("The data cannot settle this") say the second branch is open.

title: Title and Contribution 1 headline a post hoc, unvalidated test; its power, its learnability condition and its confounds are not shown
quote: A Direction-Free Test of Verifier Adaptation
explanation: The title, the abstract ("We propose a test that separates the two") and Contribution 1 present the r_t test as the paper's main methodological contribution, and say it "separates" mathematics from verifier learning and "applies to RLVR as well as to SFT". §5.3 itself says the four checks "were defined post hoc here; we offer them as a protocol for future studies, not as tested methods", and "We have not run it on RL checkpoints." Nowhere does the paper show the test can detect adaptation. There is no positive control: no run, synthetic or real, in which the model is known to learn a verifier-accepted form and r_t falls. So a flat r_t cannot be told apart from a test with no power. Two validity conditions are also left open. (1) Learnability: r_t can fall only if V accepts some correct form on the problems the defect affects. For the gold-storage defect the bare gold is parsed to its first number (App B), so it is not shown that any correct form V accepts exists for those problems. If none does (as with the 51 unparseable golds, which "never enter the training pool"), the defect cannot be learned and a flat r_t is guaranteed. (2) Separating adaptation from drift: the re-score wraps the gold only "when the prediction contains" \boxed, so any general move away from \boxed lowers r_t mechanically. The test then has the same imitation-versus-drift ambiguity the paper uses to set aside the \boxed measure (§4.4, App G). It is also fragile to accuracy-driven changes in the problem mix, so "direction-free" holds only to a first approximation. Applying it to public RLVR checkpoints needs a known, frequent defect in *their* verifier. The defect used here is a bug in this pipeline's gold storage, not a property of math-verify, so it does not carry over. A title, abstract and contribution list that lead with this test should say plainly, at least in the abstract and Contribution 1, that it is a post hoc proposal with untested sensitivity. The defensible headline is the negative empirical result (no detectable gain, declines at high LR) together with a proposed audit.

title: The falling \boxed share is a plausible sign of adapting to the gold-storage defect, and the paper does not reconcile it with "no adaptation"
quote: A model imitating its less-boxed training data would move the same way
explanation: By App B and §3.2, the gold-storage defect rejects only correct *boxed* predictions: math-verify fully parses LaTeX only inside \boxed{}/$…$, and the re-score wraps the gold only when the prediction is boxed. So the training verifier V specifically penalises \boxed answers on compound-gold problems, and the V-filtered pool is depleted of exactly those answers. App G finds that the finished generations' \boxed share falls from above the pool's level to below it (95.6%→69.7%, 98.5%→82.9%), "which imitation of the pool and drift would both produce". Imitating a pool that V has stripped of boxed answers *is* learning what V accepts. So the paper's own style measure is consistent with adaptation to this very defect, while the abstract and conclusion state that the model does not adapt to it. The two can be reconciled: a flat r_t alongside a falling \boxed share would mean the drop in boxing is not concentrated on defect-affected answers. But the paper does not make that argument. It also does not say how much of the pool's lower \boxed share comes from the gold-storage defect rather than from truncated or cap-hit examples, as App G assumes. Without this, the conclusion's pairing of "cannot separate imitation from drift" with "does not learn to avoid it" is internally loose. Suggested check: report the \boxed share separately on compound-gold versus other problems over rounds.

title: "Finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate" drops the matched-metric caveats and mixes run types
quote: 5–11 points less accurate
explanation: The abstract states as fact, without marking it post hoc, that at the highest rate finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate. Contribution 4 says "finished generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same problems". The evidence (Table 5 "Finished, matched", Table 11, App H) carries caveats that neither statement keeps. (a) The metric is post hoc and "conditions on an outcome of training and is descriptive, not a causal effect" (App H). (b) It is not "on the same problems": 22–45 of the 150 problems with no finished last-round sample drop out, the rest are reweighted, and for 6–21 problems the baseline is replaced by all-sample accuracy, which biases it. (c) The 5.5–10.6 range covers six runs, including the two no-filter runs. Those have no verifier in the loop and 3–4× the optimizer steps, and the top value (−10.6) is no-filter seed 1. Verifier-filtered self-training alone gives 5.5–9.1. The replicate and 1,024-limit runs at the same rate (App H: −5.0, −5.7) are left out. (d) One of the six intervals (A seed 2, [−11.7, 0.1]) includes zero. (e) The abstract places the phrase right after "accuracy falls in every run", which includes GSM8K Run C (−12.1 matched) and train-on-gold (−25.6/−25.9), both outside 5–11. So the scope of "5–11" is unclear. (f) Table 7's "Finished" decomposition part, a different quantity, is only −2.7 to −6.0 at the same rate. Readers may mix the two up, and the abstract does not say which one it reports. Suggested wording: "in a post hoc matched comparison, finished generations of verifier-filtered runs at the highest rate are 5.5–9.1 points less accurate (one of four intervals reaching zero)".

title: Introduction and Contribution 4 present the cap-hit rise without the conclusion's "clearly only at one seed" caveat
quote: the cap-hit share rises only at that rate
explanation: The introduction says what appears at the highest rate is lower finished accuracy "and more generations that run out of tokens". Contribution 4 says "the cap-hit share rises only at that rate". Both read as a finding that holds across runs at 5×10−4. App H and Table 7 show otherwise: at seed 1 the rise in A (+3.0 [−1.7, 7.7]) and no-filter (+2.3 [−2.5, 6.8]) has an interval including zero, "about the size of two samplings of the untrained model", and the replicate (−0.2) and the 1,024-limit run (+0.7) "do not rise at all". Termination contributes "clearly only at one seed", and the cap-share part ranges from 12–30% to 52–72% depending on seed/partition. The conclusion and App H state this correctly. The introduction and Contribution 4 should carry the same caveat (e.g. "rises clearly only at the highest rate and at one of two seeds"). Otherwise the front matter suggests a robust termination effect that the evidence does not support.

title: "Nor does it improve" and "negative on the first branch" treat a failure to detect a gain as evidence of absence, and quote the 2.2-point bound on the scale the paper says is shrunk
quote: Our answer is negative on the first branch.
explanation: The abstract ("Nor does it improve.") and the introduction ("Our answer is negative on the first branch") state a negative. The evidence supports only "no gain detected". §5.1 and the conclusion say so ("Not detectably"; the bound is "not an equivalence test"), and on pass@1 and pass@k the upper interval ends reach +8.0 and +7.3, so moderate gains on the pre-registered measures are not excluded. The abstract's 2.2-point bound has three problems. It uses sample accuracy, which was chosen as primary after the runs. It is read off observed intervals. And it is on the original-verifier scale, which App B says shrinks "every original-verifier difference and interval, including the 2.2-point bound on gains, which on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points". The abstract mentions only training-seed variance. A reader of the abstract would take 2.2 points as a calibrated upper bound on the true effect. The abstract should say "no detectable gain", mark sample accuracy as post hoc, and give the bound as ≈3 points on the corrected scale, or at least flag that the verifier defect shrinks it. The 0.73–0.78 understatement factor is itself estimated from three self-training runs only (App B: "an extrapolation from these three").

title: "On the four measures fixed in advance no run improves detectably": two of the four measures have no notion of improvement or no interval
quote: no run improves detectably
explanation: The four pre-set measures (§1) are pass@1, pass@k, \boxed style share, and per-problem transitions. Only pass@1 and pass@k have bootstrap intervals (Table 5), so "detectably" is defined only for them. Style is not a measure of mathematical improvement at all. Transitions are reported as raw added/lost counts with no interval, and §5.1 states that "In every MATH-500 run but one, the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained". For example, Run A seed 3 at 10−4 has 16 added / 14 lost (Table 4), a net gain on that measure. The conclusion's sentence extends a claim established for two measures to all four. It should say "neither pass@1 nor pass@k improves detectably in any run, and transitions are net-negative in all but one MATH-500 run".

title: Abstract calls both controls "underpowered"; the no-filter control is dose-confounded, not underpowered, and shows a directional result
quote: that patch a rarer defect or remove the filter are underpowered and show
explanation: "Underpowered" fits the \dfrac patch, whose treatment changes 0–4 training examples (§4.3, App F). It does not describe the no-filter control. That control changes the training data massively (1,400 unfiltered examples against about 440 filtered, 3–4× the optimizer steps), so its problem is a dose/data confound, not a weak treatment (App G: "dose and data differ at once"). It is also not simply "no consistent difference": removing the filter lowers pass@4 at both seeds (−2.0, −5.3), and one sample-accuracy interval excludes zero in favour of the filter (−5.5 [−9.2, −1.8] at seed 2). The conclusion describes this more accurately ("removing the filter lowers pass@4 at both seeds, within noise; single-seed intervals sometimes exclude zero"). The abstract should say the no-filter control is confounded by dose and weakly favours the filter on pass@4.

title: Three different figures for the defect's rejection share (15.5–18.4%, "about one in six", 17%/20% of pass@1) rest on different denominators
quote: 20% throughout at 10−5
explanation: The abstract and §3.2 give 15.5–18.4% of V′-accepted generations over all 500 problems. The introduction and conclusion round this to "about one in six". §5.3 and App B then add that, as a share of re-scored exam pass@1, the defect rejects 17% at seed 1 but "20% throughout at 10−5". That is one in five, outside the 15.5–18.4% band quoted as "every round" of the same runs. The difference comes from denominators: all samples on 500 problems versus first-sample pass@1 on the 150-problem exam. The paper does not say this, and §5.3 puts the two figures side by side as if they measured the same r_t. This matters because r_t's flatness is the main evidence for the "no adaptation" claim. The paper should state which denominator defines r_t, give r_t per round and per run in a table, and explain why the exam share differs.

title: r_t does fall in every re-scored run; 'no downward trend' is contradicted by the paper's own data
quote: at 10−5), with no downward trend; as a share of re-scored pass@1 it is 17% at
explanation: I recomputed r_t per round from the saved re-score files (experiments/viec3/review_cpu/patched/*.json, the same files patch_dose.py produced, all 500 problems). Run A 5e-4 seed 1: 18.3% → 16.8% → 15.7%. Seed 2: 18.1% → 17.6% → 15.5%. Run A 1e-5 seed 0: 18.3 → 17.8 → 17.5 → 16.8 → 16.8%. The series never rises from one round to the next in any of the three runs, and '15.5–18.4%' is just the range from first to last round. A problem-level paired bootstrap of the change from first to last round (2,000 resamples, problems as clusters) gives −2.6 [−5.3, +0.3] and −2.6 [−5.2, +0.1] points at 5e-4, and −1.5 [−2.9, −0.1] at 1e-5. The last interval excludes zero. By the paper's own decision rule ('r_t should fall if the model adapts'), the data point weakly toward adaptation, not against it. The headline reading 'does not fall … does not adapt' therefore does not follow from the numbers. At minimum the paper must report the per-round values and intervals and say that r_t declined. Findings 2–3 suggest the decline comes from unboxing and composition rather than adaptation, but the paper does not make that argument either.

title: The defect is fixed by the problem, so the model can avoid it only by giving up the box (or a correct answer)
quote: the bare gold is parsed to its first number and no longer
explanation: App B says the failure comes from the stored gold. For a compound gold such as 6\sqrt{2} or 137 \frac{1}{2}, the bare gold is parsed to its first number, so no correct boxed prediction can match it. Whether a correct sample is rejected depends on the problem, not on how the model writes. The saved data confirm this. Across the three runs, 54–62 problems ever produce a flip. On those problems 94–98% of V'-accepted generations are rejected by V in every round, and in most rounds 0–3 problems (at most 7 at 1e-5) have both flipped and unflipped accepts. Of the few V-accepted generations on these problems, 14 of 15 (seed 1) and 51 of 69 (1e-5) contain no \boxed. So the only way to escape the defect is to write the final answer without \boxed, but only on compound-answer problems. Writing it 'better' (e.g. \frac{4}{3} instead of \frac43) changes nothing. The test therefore asks whether the model learns a conditional 'unbox on compound answers' behaviour, which is a very specific and hard adaptation. A flat r_t is close to what one expects under any amount of global verifier adaptation, so it is uninformative. The test as proposed needs a defect whose acceptance depends on the output's form (like \dfrac → \frac), not on the gold. The paper should state this validity condition explicitly. As written, it fails for the one defect actually tested.

title: Unboxed predictions enter only the denominator, so the falling \boxed share lowers r_t mechanically
quote: the gold in \boxed{} when the prediction contains one and the gold does not
explanation: V' wraps the gold only when the prediction contains \boxed. For an unboxed prediction V' = V, so it can be in the denominator (V'-accepted) but never in the numerator. r_t therefore equals (share of V'-accepts that are boxed) × (flip rate among boxed accepts). App G reports the \boxed share falling 52% → 36% (A, seed 1). In the saved data, unboxed V-accepts grow from 73/787 (9%) to 138/566 (24%) of V'-accepts at seed 1, and from 126/1543 to 197/1446 at 1e-5. Among boxed V'-accepts only, r_t is flat: 20.2% → 20.8% (seed 1) and 19.9% → 19.5% (1e-5). So all of the observed decline in r_t is the unboxing effect. This cuts both ways. (i) A model drifting away from \boxed for reasons unrelated to V would lower r_t, and the test would read that drift as adaptation. (ii) Dropping \boxed is exactly the one route that avoids this defect (finding 2), so the paper cannot tell drift from adaptation here, the same problem it concedes for the \boxed-share measure in §4.4. The test needs the numerator and denominator restricted to boxed predictions, or V' defined for every prediction, with the boxed share reported alongside.

title: Composition confound: r_t pools over problems, and its movement is set by which problems are solved
quote: rejects does not fall over rounds, so for this one defect the model does not learn
explanation: Because flips are nearly all-or-nothing per problem (finding 2), r_t ≈ (V'-accepts on the ~50 defect-eligible problems) / (V'-accepts on all problems). Any change in how accuracy is spread across problems moves r_t, whatever the model learns about V. If training hurts compound-answer (often harder) problems more, r_t falls. If it hurts simple-number problems more, r_t rises. Seed 1 shows this: flips fall 144 → 89 (−38%) while all V'-accepts fall 787 → 566 (−28%), so r_t drops even though the within-problem flip rate on eligible problems is unchanged (96.6% → 93.7%). The train-on-gold runs, which have no verifier in the loop, show r_t moving the other way, 18.2% → 21.5% and 18.0% → 20.2%. Shifts of ±2–3 points thus occur with no verifier pressure at all, the same size as the self-training changes. A valid test should be computed within problem: for example, the per-problem flip rate among V'-accepts on defect-eligible problems that are solved in both rounds, or a problem-fixed-effects estimate. The pooled statistic confounds adaptation with changes in which problems are solved.

title: Test sensitivity is not shown: no interval, no positive control, and little pressure to adapt in offline SFT
quote: it rules out strong adaptation to this defect, not weak adaptation or adaptation
explanation: The claim that the test 'rules out strong adaptation' is never quantified. (1) There is no interval. My problem-level bootstrap gives first-to-last-round changes with intervals as wide as [−5.3, +0.3] points, so a fall of about 30% relative to an 18% baseline is not excluded. The effective sample size is the ~50 eligible problems, not the ~600–1,500 generations, because flips cluster by problem. (2) There is no positive control. Nothing shows that r_t falls when a model does adapt, for example by fine-tuning on a pool filtered to remove one output-side form, or by tracking the \dfrac class, which is output-avoidable but which the 1.5B model barely uses. (3) The pressure to adapt is small. In rejection-sampling SFT a false reject only removes a sample from the pool; there is no negative gradient. At round 0 the defect excludes ~102 of ~542 correct pool examples (19%), almost all on ~50 problems. On those problems the pool keeps only the handful of unboxed accepts, against ~400 boxed examples elsewhere teaching the opposite. With restart-from-base and 1–4 rounds, even a model that fully 'learns V' from the pool would barely see the signal. (4) The paper never says how far r_t would have to fall to count as adaptation. Without such a threshold, 'strong adaptation' has no defined meaning, and 'rules out' is unsupported.

title: Different statistics are reported under one name (generation-level r_t vs exam pass@1 share)
quote: as a share of re-scored pass@1 it roughly is (6.7/40.0 and
explanation: The abstract and §3.2 give 15.5–18.4%: generation-level V'-accept shares, pooled over all 500 problems and all k samples. §5.3 and App B also cite 17% (seed 1, round 0 and round 2) and 20% throughout at 1e-5. These are (V' pass@1 − V pass@1)/V' pass@1 on the 150-problem exam, first sample only. That is a different denominator, a different subset of problems, and about 40–60 correct answers per round. Read together, '17% at round 0 and round 2' looks like a flat statistic, while the generation-level r_t for the same run falls 18.3% → 15.7%. The exam-share figure is also very noisy: one problem on a 150-problem exam is 0.67 points of pass@1, so 4.7/28.0 vs 6.7/40.0 can be equal by chance. The 20% at 1e-5 lies outside the 15.5–18.4% range quoted as covering 'every round of the three runs'. The paper should report one pre-specified statistic (the generation-level r_t with intervals) and describe the exam share as a separate descriptive figure, or drop it.

title: 'No false accepts by V'' is assumed, yet the paper's own hand check found one
quote: one prediction had an empty box
explanation: The test counts every V'-accept as correct ('share of correct solutions'). App B says the 15.5–18.4% figure 'assumes that the re-scored verifier itself accepts no wrong answer, which we did not measure'. But in the 30-flip hand check, one flip was an empty \boxed{} that V' accepted: a V' false accept, about 3% of flips (binomial 95% CI roughly 0.1–17%). Wrapping the gold also changes how compound golds parse (for example, whether 137 \frac{1}{2} is read as a mixed number or as a product). So V' can accept answers that are differently, but not equivalently, written. If V' false accepts are concentrated in some answer styles whose frequency changes over rounds, r_t moves for reasons unrelated to adaptation. The 'correct solutions' wording in the abstract and introduction should become 'V'-accepted solutions'. A hand audit of V' accepts (not only flips) is needed before r_t can be read as a false-reject rate.

title: Applying the test to RLVR does not follow without stated validity conditions
quote: should write the rejected form less often and rt should fall over training steps.
explanation: The RLVR argument assumes there is a 'rejected form' the policy can stop writing. For the one defect studied, there is not (finding 2): the rejection is set by the gold, so even strong RL pressure (zero or negative advantage on correct-but-rejected samples) can lower r_t only through problem-conditional unboxing or by changing the answer. RLVR pipelines also typically use their own answer extraction and gold formatting, so a 'known defect class' of one verifier may not exist in another. The proposal also needs within-problem computation (finding 4), restriction to predictions V' can actually re-score (finding 3), a positive control, and intervals. None of these are stated as conditions. The interpretation 'a gain with flat r_t is evidence against adaptation to that defect' also reaches less far than the abstract's framing, 'a test that separates the two': flat r_t on one defect says nothing about whether the gain is mathematics or adaptation to other verifier properties, such as reward for any parsable answer. Shao et al.'s random-reward gains, for instance, would show flat r_t with no adaptation to the verifier at all. 'It applies to RL checkpoints' should be restated as a hypothesis that holds under explicit conditions.

title: Abstract claim 'the model does not adapt to this defect' is not supported
quote: rounds: the model does not adapt to this defect. Nor does it improve.
explanation: The abstract states a flat negative. The body hedges ('rules out strong adaptation … not weak adaptation', §5.3; 'only direct test … covers one defect', App B). Taken together, the evidence does not support the categorical statement. (a) r_t actually fell in all three runs, and at 1e-5 the problem-level interval excludes zero (finding 1). (b) The defect can be avoided only by dropping \boxed on specific problems, so the test has almost no power for it (finding 2). (c) The fall is fully accounted for by unboxing and by which problems are solved (findings 3–4), and either could be adaptation or drift. (d) There is no positive control or sensitivity analysis (finding 5). The defensible statement is roughly: 'on one gold-side defect that the model could avoid only by dropping \boxed, the share of re-scored-correct solutions it rejects changes by at most a few points (falling slightly, consistent with the decline in \boxed use); the test as applied here cannot distinguish weak adaptation from drift.' The same overstatement appears in the introduction ('for that defect the model does not adapt'), §3.2 and the conclusion ('answers it for one defect'). Because this is the title contribution, the gap between the claim and the evidence is a major problem.

title: 'Correct solutions' and 'one in six' gloss over the definition of the numerator and denominator
quote: frequent defect we measured it stays at about one in six in every round of
explanation: The introduction and abstract describe r_t as 'the share of the model's own correct solutions that a known verifier defect rejects'. In fact the denominator is V'-accepted generations (finding 7), and V' differs from V only for boxed predictions (finding 3). An unboxed correct answer that V wrongly rejects can never appear in the numerator. For eligible problems the denominator mixes ~50 problems where the share is ~96% with ~230–280 where it is 0%. 'About one in six' is thus not a per-solution rejection probability. It is a mixture weight set by how many compound-gold problems the model solves. Readers will take it as a uniform false-negative rate and will expect 'adaptation' to show up as a smooth decline of that rate. The paper should present the statistic as a problem-mixture quantity and report the within-eligible flip rate (~96%) alongside it.

title: Without a positive reference, the null on gains speaks to this training recipe, not to GVT, yet the Abstract and Conclusion state it as a finding about self-training
quote: On a held-out exam, the first answer is no: on the four measures fixed in advance
explanation: Limitation J.12 (and the last sentence of §6) says no arm in any design improves on its round 0, training on reference solutions included, so 'we have no positive reference showing that this recipe can help a 1.5B model at all; the declines may partly reflect the recipe rather than self-training.' The data back this up strongly. Train-on-gold, which has no verifier and no self-generated data, loses about 20 points (Table 5), more than any GVT arm. The no-filter arm trains on mostly wrong solutions (sample accuracy is about 30%, so roughly 70% of its 1,400 examples per round are wrong) and declines about as much as the verified arm (−8.2 vs −8.3 at seed 1). At 10^−5 the adapter barely changes behaviour (J.4). So at low rates the recipe does nothing, and at high rates every arm gets worse whatever its data: correct, wrong, gold or self-generated. Other recipe-level causes the paper lists elsewhere point the same way: loss over the prompt, a 512-token training limit that truncates a quarter of the kept pool (J.9), and possible contamination with forgetting of memorised items (J.11). Under these conditions, 'no detectable gain' and 'declines at high LR' cannot be credited to the generate–verify–select loop, because the design cannot tell apart 'GVT does not help' and 'this LoRA-SFT recipe cannot help regardless of data'. The limitation names the problem but does not bound the conclusions. The Abstract still says 'Nor does it improve' directly after the GVT result. The Conclusion answers the research question ('the first answer is no') as a statement about GVT iterations. §5.1 answers 'Not detectably' without the qualification. The same gap affects the r_t null (see separate issue): a recipe that cannot raise accuracy may also be unable to adapt to the verifier. Suggested fix: state the answer as conditional on this recipe in the Abstract, §5.1 and §7 (e.g., 'under a recipe for which we have no positive reference, ...'), and say plainly that every arm declining, gold and no-filter included, points first to the training procedure. The positive control (K) should be presented as a prerequisite for reading the null, not as optional future work.

title: The direction-free r_t test has no shown power: it is unclear that the gold-storage rejection is avoidable by the model or learnable by SFT, and r_t is confounded by problem mix
quote: it rules out strong adaptation to this defect, not weak adaptation or adaptation
explanation: The paper's headline positive claim is 'the model does not adapt to this defect' (Abstract; Conclusion: 'that share does not fall, so the model does not learn to avoid it'). For a flat r_t to be evidence against adaptation, three things must hold, and none is shown. (a) Avoidability. Appendix B describes the defect as a property of how the gold is stored: a compound gold kept without a delimiter is parsed to its first number, so a correct \boxed prediction fails. Whether the rejection happens is then mostly set by which problem it is, and the paper never shows that on these problems some alternative correct form exists that V accepts (e.g., an unboxed or differently written answer). If no such form exists, r_t cannot fall whatever the model learns, and the test has zero power for this defect. (b) A learning signal. Rejection-sampling SFT never sees the rejected forms. Adaptation could only come from those problems being under-represented in the pool, which with restart-from-base and two to four rounds is a weak signal. (c) Problem-mix confounding. r_t is a ratio over V'-accepted generations, so it moves when the set of solved problems changes. Compound-answer problems are plausibly harder, so falling accuracy could lower r_t without any adaptation, or a change could cancel a real effect. No interval is given on r_t, it rests on three runs (§5.3), and it also assumes V' makes no false accepts (App B). Two different quantities are also both reported as 'the share': 15.5–18.4% over all generations, and 17%/20% 'as a share of re-scored pass@1' on the exam (§5.3). The 20% at 10^−5 lies outside the headline range, which will confuse readers. Even 'rules out strong adaptation' therefore goes further than the evidence. Without a positive control (e.g., a synthetic defect with a known avoidable alternative, where r_t is shown to fall), the Abstract's categorical 'the model does not adapt to this defect' should be softened to 'we observed no fall in r_t', with the avoidability and power caveats stated alongside.

title: 'Restart-from-base leaves compounding little room' contradicts the data-mediated compounding the paper itself argues for in Design P, and I.2 says the shrinking-pool mechanism has 'no support'
quote: round leaves compounding little room, so the absence of compounding is
explanation: J.7 and §6 present restart-from-base as limiting compounding. That holds only for parameter-level compounding. In the loop as described (§3.1), the round-t pool is generated by the round-(t−1) model, which was itself trained on a pool from the round-(t−2) model, so selection effects can still compound through the data. Appendix D says exactly this: dose 'explains at most the level of the decline, not its time course' (the largest drops come from the smallest pools), and 'Something carried through the data, such as pool composition or style, fits this acceleration better.' That is the self-reinforcing shrinking-pool mechanism, or close to it. Yet I.2 says 'The data give it no support, but they do not rule it out either', and §5.2 says they 'neither support nor rule it out'. The appendix offers some support (accelerating decline with shrinking pools, falling \boxed share, rising $-spans), even if it is not causal evidence, while the Discussion denies any support. Separately, if compounding through data is possible, the 'absence of compounding' in Design I cannot be put down to the restart design. It reflects the short loop (2–4 trained rounds), the small changes at 10^−5, and the lack of a frequent varied defect. Suggested fix: make §5.2/I.2 and App D say the same thing ('weakly consistent with but not tested'), and rewrite J.7 to separate parameter compounding (removed by the design) from data compounding (still possible, and suggested by Design P).

title: The 2.2-point 'no gain' bound is on a scale known to be shrunk by about 0.75 and omits seed variance of comparable size; §5.1, §6 and §7 state it without these corrections, and 150 problems give little power on the pre-set measures
quote: sample-accuracy intervals exclude gains above about 2.2 points
explanation: The paper credits itself correctly for calling the bound 'loose', but several quantified weaknesses are left out of the main-text answer. (1) Appendix B shows that the original verifier understates every change by a factor of about 0.73–0.78 and says the 2.2-point bound 'on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points'. §5.1, §6 and the Conclusion still report 2.2, and §6 does not list the understatement. (2) I.1 says training-seed variance is 'of the same size' (a replicate ends 3.2 points away). An interval that included it would be wider, perhaps around 5 points, so the bound is loose by a known order of magnitude, not just in principle. (3) Power. The exam has 150 problems, of which 11–18 per partition have unparseable gold and are always unsolved (App B), so the effective n is about 132–139. pass@1 is a single draw per problem (J.3 mentions this only in passing). The resulting pass@1/pass@k intervals are about ±7 points wide (upper ends +8.0 and +7.3). On the pre-set measures, gains that would count as substantial in the self-improvement literature could not be detected. Exam size and power appear nowhere in the limitations list as a limit on the 'no gain' conclusion. Since 'no gain' is one of the paper's two headline results, the Conclusion should give the corrected bound (about 3 points on the re-scored scale, wider with seed variance) and say plainly that on the pre-set pass@1/pass@k a gain of up to about 7–8 points cannot be excluded.

title: Missing or understated limitations: the learning-rate comparison is confounded with k, pool size and number of rounds, and there is only one model family (Qwen2.5), the family where spurious-reward gains are known to appear
quote: The learning-rate grid is coarse, with three
explanation: §6 and J.4 call the higher-rate grid 'coarse' with three rounds and k = 4, but leave out the consequence. Rate is not the only thing that changes across the grid. At 10^−5 the runs use k = 8 and five rounds (round-0 pool 872, about 436 steps). At the higher rates they use k = 4 and three rounds, R0–R2, which is only two trained adapters (pool about 440, about 220 steps), and 'last round' is R4 in one case and R2 in the other (Table 5). So the higher-rate arms have about half the dose and half the training rounds of the 10^−5 arms. The pass@k measure also differs (pass@8 vs pass@4), so ∆pass@k is not comparable across rates. This matters for I.1 and App D, which use 'stronger training produces larger declines' across rates as indirect support for a dose explanation of the Design P collapse: across the grid, rate and dose move in opposite directions. J.7's 'at most five rounds' also hides that most conditions have two trained rounds, which limits any compounding test (see related issue). On scope, §6 says 'one model size in Design I' but not 'one model family'. The paper motivates itself with Shao et al.'s finding that random rewards raise accuracy (§1, §5.3), a result widely reported to depend strongly on Qwen2.5 models. Contamination of MATH-500/GSM8K (J.11) is also a known concern for Qwen2.5 specifically. Whether a sub-2B model 'learns mathematics or the verifier' under GVT may well depend on the family, so this belongs in the scope limitation, next to a note that the across-rate dose-response argument is confounded.

title: The verifier conclusions skip what the no-filter arm and the r_t null say about Egashira et al.; 'no consistent difference' undersells a filter that never helps
quote: The defensible statement about the verifier is narrow: removing a format
explanation: §5.2/I.2 settle on 'removing a format defect present in under 1% of generations, or removing the filter entirely, made no consistent difference', and say that whether systematic false negatives are harmless 'as Egashira et al. find for RLVR, our data cannot say'. Two points make this reasoning incomplete. (1) Removing the filter is not a false-negative manipulation. It turns roughly 70% of training examples into false positives (wrong answers), the error type Egashira et al. find can cause plateau or collapse. The no-filter arm is never better than the filtered arm and is worse at seed 2 (sample accuracy −10.2 vs −4.7; pass@4 lower at both seeds). With 3–4× the dose this cannot be attributed causally, but 'no consistent difference' is a flat summary of a one-sided pattern. The fact that training mostly on wrong solutions does about as well as training on verified ones is itself informative: either the filter adds nothing at this dose, or the recipe dominates (see the positive-reference issue). Neither reading is discussed. (2) The r_t result is the paper's one measurement bearing on a systematic false negative, and it is qualitatively in line with Egashira et al.'s finding that systematic FNs act like noise and are not exploited. The Discussion says the data 'cannot say' anything about this while the Abstract claims 'the model does not adapt to this defect'. The paper should either explain why the r_t null does not bear on Egashira's FN finding (e.g., different paradigm, untested avoidability), or note the consistency with suitable hedges. It should also discuss the no-filter result as a false-positive manipulation.

title: Some practical suggestions are unsupported or contradicted by the paper's own evidence, and the most important lessons are left out
quote: 0.5% of the pool cannot be detected with 150 problems
explanation: I.3 rightly says that some suggestions are general good practice, but several are still written as findings. (1) 'A treatment that changes 0.5% of the pool cannot be detected with 150 problems' is a quantitative power claim with no power analysis behind it. The patch null shows non-detection, not undetectability: a small pool change could in principle have a large effect if those examples are influential. (2) 'Check that the training step changes the model (loss and output statistics after one round)' sits awkwardly with J.4, which reports that at 10^−5 'its loss does fall' while outputs barely change. On the paper's own evidence, loss is not a valid check, and only output statistics are. (3) The list leaves out the lessons the paper's evidence supports most directly: run a positive control (or at least a gold-SFT reference that improves) before reading a null (J.12, K); set the training sequence limit to at least the generation cap plus the prompt, since 24–26% of the kept pool is truncated (J.9), which plausibly teaches unfinished outputs; and give an equivalence margin in advance (J.10). (4) 'Hold out evaluation items and keep one adapter per dataset' is offered as a remedy for the Design P artefact, but App D argues selection-set scoring did not hide a decline and may have enlarged one, so the suggestion's basis is ordinary good practice, not the paper's data. Suggested fix: label each suggestion as finding-backed or general practice, and replace the loss check with output statistics.

title: The main text presents redundant measures as extra evidence: added/lost counts restate pass@k, and the 'four pre-set measures' include non-gain measures
quote: 500 run but one, the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained.
explanation: §5.1 lists 'the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained' as a separate supporting fact. §3.4 and I.1 both note that added minus lost equals 150×∆pass@k, so this 'restates the sign of the pass@k change rather than adding evidence'. That caveat appears in the appendix but not in the main-text answer, where the sentence reads as corroboration. Likewise, the Conclusion says 'on the four measures fixed in advance no run improves detectably'. Of the four pre-set measures (pass@1, pass@k, style counts, added/lost; §3.4), style is not a gain measure and added/lost duplicates pass@k, so the null actually rests on two measures: pass@1, a single draw, and pass@k. Presenting four suggests a broader and more independent null than the data give. This is a case where a main-text summary of an appendix drops a qualifier that changes how strong the evidence looks. Suggested fix: add the 'restates pass@k' caveat to §5.1 (or drop the sentence), and in §7 name the gain measures (pass@1 and pass@k) rather than 'the four measures'.

title: Seed-1 ranges for the cap-share and finished-share leave out two seed-1 runs that contradict them
quote: 62–74%, every seed-2 run 34–59%)
explanation: Appendix H says the finished-accuracy shares 'split by seed (every seed-1 run 62–74%, every seed-2 run 34–59%)', and §4.5, §5.3(ii), the Conclusion and App I.1 say the cap-share part is '12–30% of the decline at seed 1 and 52–72% at seed 2'. I recomputed these from Table 7. A,1 / B,1 / No filter,1 give finished shares of 73/62/74% and cap-share fractions of 1.3/8.3=16%, 2.0/6.7=30% and 1.0/8.2=12%, which matches the stated ranges. Seed 2 also checks out (72%, 52%, 60%). But Table 7 lists two more seed-1 runs at 5×10−4: 'A replicate, 1' (Fin. share 89%, cap-share +0.1 of −5.2, i.e. about −2%) and 'A, 1024 limit, 1' (85%, cap-share −0.3 of −5.7, i.e. about 5%). Both fall outside the stated ranges. So 'every seed-1 run 62–74%' is wrong as written. The 12–30% figure holds only for the three original-configuration seed-1 runs and should say so. This matters because the text reads the split by seed as 'partition variation'. The two extra seed-1 runs show that same-partition runs also reach 85–89%, which weakens that reading and widens the seed-1 cap-share range to about −2% to 30%.

title: A seed-0 sample-accuracy interval with upper end 0.0 is described as excluding zero
quote: exclude zero (upper ends −0.6 and 0.0 for sample accuracy, −0.5 and −0.9
explanation: In Table 5, the 10−5 sample-accuracy interval for A, seed 0 is −2.4 [−4.8, 0.0]. An interval that ends at 0.0 does not exclude zero. Appendix E contradicts itself here. It first says sample accuracy falls 'with one interval (B, seed 0) excluding zero', then says 'These seed-0 intervals only just exclude zero (upper ends −0.6 and 0.0 for sample accuracy ...)', which counts A's [−4.8, 0.0] as excluding zero. §4.2 likewise says 'sample accuracy falls 1.2–3.2 points and matched finished accuracy 1.1–4.2, with intervals that only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0', which a reader will take to cover both measures. title: Understatement factor 0.73–0.78 does not fit all re-scored runs and does not rescale intervals
quote: same factor shrinks every original-verifier difference and interval, including the
explanation: The factor is defined as 'the ratios of original to re-scored sample-accuracy changes below'. For the three self-training runs the ratios are −8.3/−10.7=0.78, −4.7/−6.0=0.78 and −2.4/−3.3=0.73, so 0.73–0.78 is right for them. The same paragraph also gives the train-on-gold changes (−19.7 vs −24.7 and −18.7 vs −22.0, repeated in App G), and those ratios are 0.80 and 0.85, outside the range. The stronger claim, that 'the same factor shrinks every original-verifier difference and interval, including the 2.2-point bound on gains, which on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points', does not match the re-scored intervals the paper reports. Interval widths change by ratios of 0.92–0.96, not 0.73–0.78 (A,1: 7.8 vs 8.1; A,2: 7.0 vs 7.5; A 10−5: 4.8 vs 5.2). The upper endpoints shift down rather than scale: [−4.8, 0.0] becomes [−5.9, −0.7], and [−8.2, −1.2] becomes [−9.7, −2.2]. Dividing +2.2 by about 0.75 to get 'nearer 3' therefore has no basis in these data. In addition, the 2.2 endpoint comes from the 10−4 runs (seeds 1 and 3), which were never re-scored.

title: The r_t evidence reports pass@1-based shares selectively; the unreported seed-2 share falls
quote: round 0 and round 2 at seed 1 and 20% throughout at 10−5 (Appendix B). This
explanation: §5.3 gives r_t as 15.5–18.4% 'in every round of the three runs', then adds pass@1-based shares of 17% (seed 1) and 20% (10−5). The 20% lies outside the 15.5–18.4% range. The two figures use different denominators: re-scored exam pass@1 versus all V'-accepted generations on 500 problems. The text does not flag this, so a reader sees two contradictory numbers for the same quantity. The third run is also left out. From App B's figures, Run A at 5×10−4 seed 2 has re-scored pass@1 38.0→32.0 and original 31.3→27.3. Its offsets are 6.7 and 4.7, so the pass@1-based share moves from 6.7/38.0=17.6% to 4.7/32.0=14.7%. That is the one downward move in these data, the direction the test reads as adaptation, and it falls below the stated range. pass@1 is a noisy single draw, but quoting the share for seed 1 and 10−5 and omitting seed 2 makes the 'no downward trend' evidence look more uniform than the paper's own numbers show. The r_t values per run and round on the stated denominator should be given, ideally in a table.

title: §4.1 says selection problems fall as much as the exam; App D's numbers show they sometimes fall less
quote: fall as much as the exam)
explanation: §4.1 defends Design P's selection-set scoring by saying 'in Design I the selection problems fall as much as the exam'. Appendix D's own comparison is mixed. At 10−5, selection falls less (−1.0 and −1.1 against exam −2.4 and −1.4). Run C at 5×10−4 falls clearly less (−11.3 against −15.4). Run A at 5×10−4 seed 1 is −8.2 against −8.3, and only 10−4 seed 1 (−6.2 vs −1.5) and 5×10−4 seed 2 (−5.3 vs −4.7) fall more. App D's phrase 'as much as or more than ... at the two higher rates' is also loose: there are three higher rates, the examples are drawn from 5×10−4 and 10−4, and −8.2 vs −8.3 is slightly less. The main-text summary should match App D's mixed result. A smaller point: App D's exam values (−1.4, −15.4, −13.0) do not match Table 5 (A,1 −1.5; C,1 −15.3; C,0 −13.1). The differences are only rounding, but the paper should use one source.

title: Abstract's '5–11 points' covers only some of the runs that 'every run' refers to
quote: come 5–11 points less accurate
explanation: The abstract says 'At the highest rate accuracy falls in every run, and finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate'. The 5–11 range (5.5–10.6 in Table 5) comes from the six MATH-500 verifier-filtered and no-filter runs. Other runs at 5×10−4 fall outside it. Train-on-gold loses 25.6 and 25.9 points of matched finished accuracy, and the GSM8K Run C at 5×10−4 loses 12.1. Read literally, 'every run' at the highest rate includes those three, so the range is too narrow. Saying 'the six MATH-500 self-training and no-filter runs' would fix it. The intro states its scope correctly ('what training at the highest rate changes ... 5.5–10.6'), but the abstract does not.

title: Table 11 gives the same round-0 length for two different exam partitions
explanation: In Table 11, both 10−5 rows (A, seed 0 and A, seed 1) have round-0 mean length 1158 characters (1158 →1147 and 1158 →1146). Seeds 0 and 1 draw different 150-problem exam partitions, and their round-0 cap-hit shares (46.9% vs 40.7%) and finished accuracies (54.8% vs 55.2%) differ. With cap-hit six points apart, an identical mean length to the character is unlikely. Elsewhere, different partitions give different round-0 lengths (1175, 1154, 1178). This may be a transcription error and should be checked.

title: Novelty claim overstated: Egashira et al. and TinyV already measure the verifier's false-negative rate on the policy's own outputs step by step, and Egashira et al. use it to test whether the model adapts
quote: TinyV and Huang et al. measure false-reject rates to repair or compare verifiers, and Egashira et al. inject hand-designed error patterns
explanation:
The paper says its main proposed contribution is new: a per-round measurement of the verifier's false-reject rate on the loop's own outputs, used as a test of whether the model adapts to the verifier (§2: "Nor did we find, in the studies above, a per-round measurement of the verifier’s false-reject rate on the loop’s own outputs"; App. A Positioning; Contributions in §1). I checked the cited papers directly. Two of them already do close to this, and App. A describes both inaccurately.

(a) Egashira et al. (arXiv:2605.02909, https://arxiv.org/html/2605.02909). In §4.1 they compute unbiased estimates of reward, FPR and FNR from the policy's own rollouts at every training step, and Fig. 2 plots FNR/FPR over steps. For systematic false negatives, including a format-based one, they report that 'the model first unlearns behavior that triggers false negatives and then receives valid training signal' (§4.2) and that 'the model can learn to avoid outputs that trigger those false negatives' (§3). That is exactly a test of verifier adaptation through the step-wise false-reject rate on the loop's own outputs, with a positive result in RLVR. Saying they only 'inject hand-designed error patterns' leaves out the measurement that matters most here. The real difference is that the paper applies the measurement to a naturally occurring defect, in offline SFT, using a repaired verifier as the reference. That is a smaller difference than the paper claims.

(b) TinyV (arXiv:2505.14625, https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14625). §4.1 / Figs. 3–4 re-annotate every GRPO rollout of Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B with LLM judges and track false negatives of the rule-based Prime Verifier over training steps. The FN-affected prompt fraction 'increases steadily after the first epoch' (46.7% / 50.5% cumulative), the per-step FN ratio averages about 20% of rollouts, and the authors attribute the growth to 'the model exploring diverse answer formats that Prime Verifier fails to recognize'. This is a per-step false-reject measurement on the loop's own outputs, read in terms of the model's answer format moving relative to the verifier. Saying TinyV only measures false-reject rates 'to repair or compare verifiers' is inaccurate.

(c) Less directly, Cai et al. (arXiv:2510.00915, §3.3) estimate the FN rate online during training by appealing a random subset of the step-t rule-based negatives to an LLM checker. They do not report the trajectory (App. C.4 gives only aggregates), but the measurement itself exists.

The defensible claim is narrower. It would be something like: the first application of a step-wise false-reject audit to a naturally occurring, pipeline-specific defect in offline rejection-sampling SFT, framed as a test that does not depend on the direction of accuracy. Egashira et al. and TinyV should be credited as precedents for the measurement, in §2, App. A and the Contributions.

title: Related work omits prior results that bear directly on how to read the flat r_t (RL models do adapt to format-based false negatives; FN rates can rise over training)
quote: Our setting differs in paradigm (oﬄine rejection-sampling SFT with a fresh adapter per round, not on-policy RL) and in task (real benchmark problems). Our patch control cannot test their false-negative finding
explanation: App. A cites Egashira et al. only for 'systematic false negatives behave like random noise' and says the paper's controls cannot test that finding. It leaves out the result that matters most for the proposed r_t test. In RLVR, Egashira et al. observe the model actively unlearning behaviour that triggers a format-based false negative (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.02909, §4.2), so the FNR falls. TinyV observes the opposite trend under GRPO: false negatives accumulate as the policy explores answer formats the verifier does not parse (https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14625, §4.1). Taken together, prior work shows that the step-wise false-reject rate can fall (adaptation) or rise (format drift) during RL. The paper's flat r_t (15.5–18.4%) is a third pattern. It needs to be set against these and explained. An obvious candidate explanation is the paradigm difference the paper itself names. Rejection-sampling SFT never gives a gradient against rejected samples; it only drops them. So adaptation can happen only if the accepted pool's format distribution shifts and the next fresh adapter imitates that shift. RL with negative advantages pushes probability away from rejected outputs directly. Without this comparison, a reader may take 'the model does not adapt to this defect' as a general property of verifier adaptation rather than a property of this paradigm and dose. This also weakens §1/§5.3's claim that the test 'applies to RLVR as well as to SFT' as a new tool: in RLVR, Egashira et al. have already run it.

title: "They do not ask what the gain consists of" is contradicted by the cited RLVR papers themselves
quote: These studies improve accuracy, which our SFT loop does not, but they do not ask what the gain consists of.
explanation: The first cited example is Wang et al.'s 36.0%→73.6% on MATH-500 (verified, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20571, NeurIPS 2025). Its own abstract decomposes that gain: it reports an '8.6% improvement beyond format correction', which implies most of the jump is format correction. That is the same 'mathematics or format/verifier?' question this paper poses, answered in part by the cited authors. In the sibling cluster, SimpleRL-Zoo (arXiv:2503.18892) analyses response length, reasoning behaviours and format-reward effects across its ten base models. Huang et al. (arXiv:2505.22203), from the same group, studies how rule-based-verifier false negatives shape RL gains. The statement is therefore inaccurate as written. It also hides a useful fact for the paper's motivation: the headline 1.5B RLVR number cited in §1 and §2 is largely a format effect by its authors' own account. That supports the paper's framing better than the current wording, which presents 36.0→73.6 as an unexamined accuracy gain. Suggested change: report the 8.6-point beyond-format figure, and narrow the claim to 'do not test whether the gain reflects adaptation to the verifier's specific defects'.

title: Qiao et al. described as purely theoretical and out of its multi-silo setting
quote: Qiao et al. [8] argue theoretically that a selector seeing only a narrow slice of the target distribution accelerates collapse.
explanation: Qiao et al. (arXiv:2606.13732, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13732) prove the result and also run experiments. Their setting is siloed selection, where each of several verifiers or institutions sees only a local, biased slice and raw data cannot be pooled, and they propose Wasserstein proxy references as a fix. 'Argue theoretically' undersells the empirical part. Leaving out the multi-silo framing makes the result look more directly applicable to a single rule-based verifier with a format bias than it is. A single format-biased verifier is a different kind of selection bias: it depends on the answer form, not on a local view of the distribution. This is minor, but the main-text paraphrase 'a narrow selector can accelerate collapse' should state the setting.

title: §4.1 overstates the selection-vs-exam check; at Design P's own learning rate the selection problems fell less, and the differences are within noise
quote: set scoring is unlikely to have masked a decline (in Design I the selection problems
explanation: The main text says that in Design I the selection problems 'fall as much as the exam'. Appendix D does not support that as a blanket statement. Selection falls as much or more only at the two higher rates (5e-4: -8.2/-5.3 vs -8.3/-4.7; 1e-4 seed 1: -6.2 vs -1.5). At 1e-5 Run A's selection problems fall less (-1.0 and -1.1 against -2.4 and -1.4/-1.5), less than half the exam decline at seed 0. Run C at 5e-4 also falls less (-11.3 vs -15.4). The rate that matters here is 1e-5, because Design P was trained at 1e-5. At that rate, and for Run A, the comparison leans the other way: training on a problem's own accepted solutions may have partly protected it. Second, Appendix D gives no intervals for these selection-minus-exam differences. With 150 exam problems the sample-accuracy changes alone have intervals about ±2.5–4 points wide (Table 5), so gaps of 1–2 points (and even the 4.7-point gap at 1e-4 seed 1, which has no interval) cannot tell 'falls more', 'as much' and 'less' apart. The honest summary is 'no detectable difference, with a hint of protection at 1e-5'. That supports 'unlikely to have masked' only weakly. It does not support App D's further remark that selection scoring 'may have enlarged' the decline, which rests on noise-level gaps at other rates. The main text should match the appendix: mixed results, slightly less decline at 1e-5, no intervals.

title: Sample-accuracy interval for A, seed 0 does not exclude zero, yet §4.2 and App E say it does
quote: matched finished accuracy 1.1–4.2, with intervals that only just exclude zero for
explanation: §4.2 says the sample-accuracy and matched finished-accuracy intervals 'only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0'. In Table 5 the sample-accuracy interval for A, seed 0 is [-4.8, 0.0]. Its upper end is 0.0, so it includes zero, or at best touches it. Only B, seed 0 ([-5.9, -0.6]) excludes zero. Appendix E first says this correctly ('one interval (B, seed 0) excluding zero'). A few lines later it says 'These seed-0 intervals only just exclude zero (upper ends -0.6 and 0.0 for sample accuracy ...)', which contradicts itself because an upper end of 0.0 does not exclude zero. Both lists of upper ends also switch order: -0.6 and 0.0 is B then A, while -0.5 and -0.9 matched is A then B. The right count is: for sample accuracy, 1 of 4 MATH-500 intervals excludes zero at 1e-5; for matched finished accuracy, 2 of 4 do, both at seed 0, and the paper itself calls those two close to one replicate. The main text should say this and not merge the two metrics. The conclusion ('possible small decline, not an established one') survives, but the evidence is weaker than §4.2 suggests.

title: 'The adapter barely changes the outputs' at 1e-5 rests on coarse aggregates and conflicts with the paper's own decline and divergence evidence
quote: on MATH-500 the adapter barely changes the outputs (length and cap-hit share
explanation: This claim carries a lot of weight. It is used to say the flat MATH-500 curve at 1e-5 is uninformative (§4.2), to explain the null patch control (§4.3, App F: 'nearly identical pools would give nearly identical models'), and it motivates the higher-rate runs (§4.4). The only evidence given is that mean length (1158->1147) and cap-hit share (46.9->47.4%, 40.7->41.8%) barely move for Run A. Those are coarse summaries: an adapter can change which answers are produced, the reasoning, or the style while leaving length and termination unchanged. The paper's own data show outputs did change in ways that matter. Finished accuracy goes 54.8->51.0 (Table 11). Matched finished accuracy falls 3.8 and 4.2 points with intervals excluding zero at seed 0. All-agree shares fall (14.6->12.0%). The paper reads the decline as a 'possible small decline', which implies the model changed. Either the 1e-5 declines are real, and then the adapter changed the outputs, or the outputs did not change, and then the declines are noise. The paper uses both readings in different places. The supporting evidence that 'the adapter therefore learns' (training loss 0.72->0.38) is also weak for this purpose: §3.4 says loss is computed over the whole chat sequence including the fixed prompt, so part of that drop may just be fitting the repeated template. To support the claim, a direct output-level measure is needed, for example \boxed/$ style shares by round at 1e-5 (as reported for the higher rates), per-problem added/lost churn compared with a resampling-of-base baseline, or token-level divergence between round-0 and round-4 generations. Otherwise 'little change' should be stated as an inference from length and cap-hit only.

title: 'Little change is a property of rate and steps together' is concluded from a comparison confounded by dataset
quote: is therefore a property of rate and steps together, not of the rate alone. A flat
explanation: Appendix E concludes that 'little change' depends on steps as well as rate, because Run C, at the same rate with about twice the steps (951 vs 436), does change its outputs. Run C is also the only GSM8K run. It differs from Run A in dataset, in base accuracy (66.7% vs 32%), and in cap-hit regime (3.5% vs 41–48%). The same appendix and §4.2 explicitly decline to attribute Run C's decline to the dataset alone, for exactly this reason. Attributing Run C's larger output change to steps is the mirror-image inference and needs the same hedge. Run C's time course also does not fit a per-round dose effect well: 9.3 of its 12.7 pass@1 points are lost in the final round, while the per-round dose is roughly constant or shrinking. App D then cites this inference ('Run C ... is the one 10^-5 run that declines clearly') as support for the Design P dose reading, so the conclusion rests on a single confounded comparison. It should be stated as one possible reading, not as a finding.

title: The 'dose explains level, not acceleration' argument is a false dichotomy, and dose does not even explain the level at round 1
quote: Dose also explains at most the level of the decline, not its time course: with a
explanation: The arithmetic checks out: the two largest pass@1 drops (-12.1 = 44.5->32.4 and -13.8 = 32.4->18.6) come from models trained on the pools of 3,395 and 2,638 examples. The inference drawn from it does not hold. (a) Dose and compounding through data interact rather than compete. Under restart-from-base, a larger per-round dose makes each round's model imitate its pool more strongly, so whatever drift is in the pool passes into the next generation faster. A high dose can therefore produce acceleration even while pool sizes shrink, so 'dose explains at most the level' does not follow. (b) The level is not explained by dose either. The round-1 model received the largest dose (3,962 examples, about 4.5x Run A) yet fell only 3.8 points (50.0->46.2), about the same as Design I Run A's round-1 drop of 2.7–5.3 points at 1x dose. On the dose reading the early level should differ most, and it does not. Together these suggest the collapse emerges over rounds, which fits a data-borne compounding mechanism amplified by dose more than either alone. The paper reaches a similar view ('something carried through the data ... fits this acceleration better'), but its stated reason splits the two mechanisms. The 1.5B pool shrinks by 60% (3,962->1,566) while the 0.5B pool shrinks only 16% (2,533->2,123); this is a further signal of compounding that could be used and is not discussed.

title: The 0.5B Design P run is the natural within-design control but is underused and has no uncertainty attached
quote: declines only a little, though it is a different model. Pooling or scoring may also
explanation: The 0.5B and 1.5B Design P runs share both structural features the paper lists as alternative explanations: pooled training on one adapter, and scoring on the selection set. The 0.5B run also has a large dose (2,533 examples, about 2.9x Run A, not far from the 1.5B's 4.5x). It shows only a mild, roughly linear decline (pass@1 -3.7, pass@8 -5.6) and little pool contraction. This is the strongest evidence in the paper that pooling and selection scoring are not sufficient on their own to produce the collapse. Yet App D closes with 'Pooling or scoring may also have contributed' without confronting it, and dismisses the 0.5B comparison only with 'it is a different model'. Several things are missing for 0.5B that are given for 1.5B: a per-dataset split (Table 9), style counts, a per-round pool trajectory (only the endpoints 2,533 to 2,123), and any interval on its decline. The main text calls the decline 'small' with no interval, even though the paper insists elsewhere on bootstrap intervals and patterns across runs. Either analyse the 0.5B run as the partial control it is, which narrows the candidate causes to model-by-dose interaction or compounding, or state clearly that it was not analysed and why.

title: Exam declines quoted in App D's selection-set comparison do not match Table 5
quote: less (−1.0 and −1.1 against −2.4 and −1.4), and Run C’s selection problems
explanation: App D compares selection-set declines with exam declines, but three of the exam figures differ from Table 5's sample-accuracy column. Run A, 1e-5, seed 1 is -1.4 in App D and -1.5 in Table 5. Run C at 5e-4 is -15.4 in App D ('-11.3 against -15.4') and -15.3 in Table 5. Run C at 1e-5 is -13.0 in App D ('-13.8 against -13.0') and -13.1 in Table 5. The differences are probably due to the separate re-scoring mentioned in Appendix C, but App D does not say which scoring it uses, and the same comparison mixes figures that do match Table 5 (-8.3, -4.7, -1.5 at 1e-4) with figures that do not. App D should state the scoring source or use the Table 5 values. These gaps are small, but they are the same size as the selection-minus-exam differences the argument relies on (e.g. -13.8 vs -13.0 is reported as 'slightly more').

title: Answer-diversity measures: stated scope contradicted by reported values, and the handling of cap-hit (no-answer) generations is unspecified
quote: (0.542 →0.554 for Run A, seed 0; 0.528 →0.543 for Run B, seed 1) but rises
explanation: App F says diversity was measured 'for Design P's 1.5B run and the 10^-5 Design I runs at seed 0'. The distinct-answer fraction is then reported for 'Run B, seed 1', which lies outside that scope. Either the scope or the label is wrong, and A and B are compared at different seeds and different partitions. More substantively, 41–48% of MATH-500 generations hit the token cap and mostly have no extractable answer, and in Design P \boxed usage halves. Neither the all-agree measure nor the distinct-answer measure says how a missing or unextractable answer is counted: as its own 'answer', as distinct each time, or excluded. That choice can by itself drive the reported movements, for example Design P's distinct fraction rising 0.443->0.712 and all-agree falling 24.8->1.7% as formatting drifts. The paper notes the link to cap-hits but gives no rule. Mixing selection and exam problems in Design I also mixes problems the model trained on with held-out ones. The paper draws no conclusion from these measures, which is appropriate, but the definitions need to be given for the numbers to be interpretable or reproducible.

title: Table 2's round-3 pass@8 corresponds to the default preset, contradicting 'the two presets gave identical pooled values'
quote: identical pooled values; a later per-dataset recomputation differs by one prob-
explanation: App D says Table 2 was computed during the run, 'where the two verifier presets gave identical pooled values'. Table 9's caption says that after recomputation the pooled round-3 pass@8 is 63.5% under the reward preset (the one used for selection, and per §3.4 the definition of 'correct') and 63.6% under the default preset. 63.6% is the value in Table 2. Recomputing from Table 9's per-dataset reward values gives (82.2+44.8)/2 = 63.5. So Table 2's R3 pass@8 matches the default preset rather than the reward preset. This is a one-problem difference with no effect on conclusions, but the 'identical' statement and the convention that 'correct' means the reward preset are not exactly true for Table 2. The caption could say which preset Table 2 uses. All other Table 2 entries reproduce exactly as averages of Table 9's two datasets, and all Table 2, 3 and 9 deltas recompute correctly.

title: Train-on-gold collapse at 5×10⁻⁴ means the 5×10⁻⁴ declines cannot be read as evidence about self-training or the verifier
quote: At 5×10−4 every run declines: pass@1 falls 4.0–11.3 points
explanation: I recomputed every 5×10⁻⁴ delta from Tables 4, 6 and 10, and they match Table 5: A −10.0/−4.0, B −4.7/−11.3 pass@1; no-filter −6.0/−8.7; gold −18.0/−21.3 pass@1 and −20.7/−20.7 pass@4. The problem is what the controls imply. Training once on the 350 correct, verifier-independent reference solutions, for about the same number of steps as Run A (175 against 220/196), drops pass@4 from 50.0 to 33.3 (seed 1) and from 51.3 to 28.7 (seed 2) after a single adapter (Table 6, R1). So at this rate, under this recipe (loss over the prompt, terse references, no warmup), one epoch of SFT on clean off-policy data badly damages the model. Removing the verifier (no-filter) gives a decline as large as or larger than the filtered run. Neither the filter nor the source of the data separates the outcomes, which is the pattern expected if 5×10⁻⁴ sits in a regime where the update itself does damage whenever the training data departs from the base model's own distribution. Tables 6 and 10 also show a specific pattern: the first self-training adapter (R1, trained on the base model's own accepted outputs) is nearly flat (A pass@1 32.7/31.3, B 35.3/31.3), and the decline appears only at R2. Because adapters restart from base, the R2 adapter differs from R1 only in being trained on the outputs of an already-shifted model, i.e. more off-distribution data. That is the same mechanism that wrecks train-on-gold in one step. The paper hedges ('describe rather than identify causes'), but the abstract and §4.4/§4.5 still present 'at the highest rate accuracy falls in every run' and the anatomy as findings about GVT self-training. The gold control is never used to say what it most directly shows: at 5×10⁻⁴ the recipe is fragile, so these declines say little about self-training or verifier adaptation specifically. The R1-flat/R2-decline pattern is also unreported, though it is the most informative within-run fact here. A sentence that frames 5×10⁻⁴ as an optimisation-fragile regime, and that reports the R1/R2 pattern, would make the section's conclusions match its evidence.

title: 'Mostly real' argument for the train-on-gold decline is not bounded by the checks offered
quote: fall of about 19 points, and finished accuracy falls to 12–15%, so we think the fall
explanation: The concern is that the gold-trained model shifts strongly in format ($-spans 5%→98%, \boxed 52%→86%), and the same verifier grades the result. The paper offers three supports. (i) An exact-string match on boxed answers recovers 14/600 and 11/600 (≈2.3 and 1.8 points; checked). This is a lower bound, and the paper says so. (ii) The gold-storage re-score fixes a different defect, which the paper also concedes. (iii) Finished accuracy falls to 12–15% (Table 11: 14.7, 12.5). But (iii) is not independent evidence: finished accuracy is graded by the same verifier, so if the new style is misparsed it is misparsed in finished generations too. Nothing bounds the error from above. The ≈14% of round-2 generations with no \boxed are where math-verify falls back to the last LaTeX/$ span, and in a $-heavy reference style that span is often not the final answer. Those generations alone could account for up to ~14 points, and with the 2-point lower bound that is ~16 of the ~19-point fall. Equivalent-but-not-string-equal boxed answers are also uncounted. 'Even several times the first bound' is an arbitrary multiplier, not a bound. The conclusion may well be right, but a hand audit of a small random sample (e.g. 50 rejected round-2 generations per seed) is needed to support 'mostly real'. Otherwise the claim should be weakened to 'the share of verifier error is unmeasured; at least ~2 points of it is recoverable'.

title: No-filter control confounds more than dose (62% truncated training data), and learning-rate dependence is used as evidence that step count matters
quote: matter (the rate dependence above is suggestive), dose and data differ at once
explanation: The no-filter vs Run A deltas check out from Table 6 (pass@1 +4.0/−4.7, pass@4 −2.0/−5.3; sample-acc +0.2/−5.5 from Table 5's round-0 values). Two problems remain. (a) The paper names only optimizer steps (700 vs 220/196, 3.2–3.6×) as the confound. Table 11 shows a second, mechanistically relevant one: 62.4% of the no-filter round-0 pool is longer than the 512-token training limit, against 24.5% for Run A. The no-filter model is thus trained mostly on examples with no final answer and no EOS, the very mechanism §H tests with the 1,024-limit arm. A 2.5× higher share of unterminated training data, plus unfiltered wrong answers, plus 3–4× the steps, makes the comparison uninterpretable as an effect of the filter. That it nonetheless barely differs from Run A at seed 1 (cap-hit +2.3 vs +3.0) is itself informative about the truncation hypothesis and deserves mention. (b) The justification 'since dose may matter (the rate dependence above is suggestive)' conflates learning rate with number of optimizer steps. The rate sweep varies step size at a fixed step count, so even a firm rate dependence would not show that step count matters. Recommend listing truncation share as a confound and dropping or rephrasing the rate→dose inference.

title: Rate dependence and 'cap-hit rises only at 5×10⁻⁴' are weaker than stated, and partly contradicted by the replicate and Table 12
quote: at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 1.5, 3.5 and 8.3 points
explanation: The values are correct (Table 5: −1.5, −3.5, −8.3 at seed 1; −3.7, −3.8, −4.7 at seed 2), and the appendix hedges ('suggestive, not established'). But the main text's 'may grow with the rate on one seed' leans on the −8.3 endpoint, and the same-configuration replicate at seed 1 and 5×10⁻⁴ gives −5.2 (Table 7). The −8.3 run is therefore an extreme of two draws differing by 3.1 points, the paper's only replicate-noise estimate. That spread exceeds the 2-point gap between 1e-4 and 2e-4 at seed 1. Table 12 is also hard to square with a rate trend. Re-scored on the same seed-1 exam, the 2×10⁻⁴ adapter's deficit to the untrained model (−7.8 at 512 tokens) is as large as the two 5×10⁻⁴ adapters' (−8.0, −8.8), and its proxy-degenerate share (28.7%) is similar to theirs (30.0%, 37.2%). Likewise, §4.4's 'The cap-hit share rises only at 5×10⁻⁴' is true only at seed 2: at seed 1 the 5×10⁻⁴ rises (+3.0 [−1.7, 7.7], +2.3, replicate −0.2, 1024-limit +0.7) are within noise, as Appendix H itself notes. The main text should say the rate dependence is not supported beyond noise at either seed, and that the cap-hit rise is a seed-2 phenomenon.

title: Attribution between 'less accurate' and 'not finishing' rests on post-treatment conditioning and an untested counterfactual
quote: round-0 samples (6–21 problems, 34–37 in the gold runs), which, being mostly
explanation: The decomposition is arithmetically sound. I checked that the three parts sum to Δacc in every Table 7 row within rounding, and reproduced A seed 1 from Table 11 (s̄=0.553, Δf=−11.0 → −6.1; implied c=7.0%→4.7% → cap-acc −1.0; Δs=−3.0 × (f̄−c̄)=42.7 → −1.3). The interpretation is less secure, for three related reasons. (1) The matched metric conditions on finishing, an outcome of training. It drops the 22–45 problems (15–30% of the exam) where every last-round sample hits the cap, i.e. the problems most affected by non-termination. Within a problem, it also compares the round-0 finished samples with a different, selected subset at the last round, since when more samples run long, the ones that still finish are not a random draw. Matching on problem does not remove that within-problem selection. (2) The fallback baseline (all-sample round-0 accuracy for 6–21 problems, 34–37 for gold) is mostly cap-hit accuracy (4–7%). This biases the baseline down and so understates the matched decline. The paper notes the bias but not its direction for the headline '5–11 points'. In the gold runs a quarter of the problems use the fallback, so −25.6/−25.9 mixes two baselines. (3) The cap-share part Δs(f̄−c̄) values every generation that stops finishing at the average finished accuracy f̄. That assumes newly unfinished generations would have been as accurate as typical finished ones, but drift-prone generations are plausibly harder or already going wrong, which would make the termination share an overstatement. Conversely, the unmatched f in the finished part contains composition shifts. The 'Fin. share' percentages therefore depend on these assumptions as much as on the data. The text is careful ('descriptive'), but the abstract's 'mostly via less accurate finished solutions, partly via more cap-hits' framing should be stated as dependent on this counterfactual, and the direction of the fallback bias should be stated.
