title: The 1,536-token re-score points to non-termination at seed 1, contrary to 'picture unchanged'
quote: cap leave the picture unchanged, within the noise of single runs (Appendix H).
explanation: At 512 tokens, the seed-1 anatomy says finished accuracy carries most of the decline (finished part 73–89% for A, replicate and 1024-limit; cap-share 12–30%). Table 12 at 1,536 tokens tells a different story for the same seed-1 adapters. Proxy 'Acc. finished' is nearly identical across rows (untrained 44.1, replicate 43.3, 1024-limit 41.3, 2e-4 40.8), while the 'Degenerate' share is 2.5% vs 23–33%. The arithmetic shows that the deficit is almost entirely the degenerate share. With degenerate generations scored ≈0, sample acc ≈ (1−deg)×acc_fin: untrained 0.975×44.1=43.0 (reported 43.2); replicate 0.77×43.3=33.3 (34.2); 1024-limit 0.673×41.3=27.8 (29.5). The −9.0 replicate deficit is thus ≈0.205×43 ≈ 8.8 points of non-termination and <1 point of finished accuracy. The proxy undercounts cap-hits, which contaminates 'Acc. finished' with low-accuracy unfinished text more for the adapters, so their true finished accuracy is if anything closer to the untrained model's. The appendix does say the re-score 'points to non-termination', but §4.5 summarises it as leaving the picture unchanged. With a larger budget the seed-1 adapters look like models that fail to stop, not models whose finished solutions are 5–9 points worse. That conflicts with the 512-token seed-1 split and with the abstract's emphasis on less accurate finished solutions. A second caveat: the untrained 512-token re-score (36.3%) is 2.6 points above the run's own round 0 (33.7%), inflating all deficits. For example, the 2×10⁻⁴ deficit is −7.8 here against −3.5 in Table 5. The §4.5 sentence should be revised, and the anatomy claim qualified by cap length.

title: Seed-1 ranges in the anatomy omit the two other seed-1 runs at 5×10⁻⁴
quote: The cap-share part is 12–30% of the decline at seed 1 and 52–72%
explanation: From Table 7, the cap-share/Δacc at seed 1 is A 1.3/8.3=16%, B 2.0/6.7=30%, no-filter 1.0/8.2=12% (hence 12–30%), and at seed 2 3.4/4.7=72%, 4.8/9.2=52%, 6.1/10.2=60% (52–72%). Both match. But Table 7 also lists two more seed-1 5×10⁻⁴ runs, the replicate (cap-share +0.1/−5.2 ≈ −2%) and the 1024-limit run (0.3/5.7 ≈ 5%), and these fall outside '12–30%'. Likewise the next sentence says 'every seed-1 run 62–74%' for the finished share, while the replicate is 89% and the 1024-limit run 85%. Including them strengthens the seed split rather than weakening it, but 'every seed-1 run' is literally false as written. The ranges should cover all seed-1 rows or state that they cover the A/B/no-filter runs only.

title: 'Three rounds' and per-round step counts include a round-2 pool that trains no evaluated model
quote: 175, against 220, 196 and 163 for Run A at seed 1 (and 212, 193, 175 at seed 2).
explanation: Rounds are R0 (untrained), R1 (adapter on the R0 pool) and R2 (adapter on the R1 pool), so 'three rounds' at the higher rates means only two trained adapters, and each restarts from base. Yet the dose comparison lists three per-round step counts (220, 196, 163 = 440/2, 391/2, 326/2), and Tables 6/10 report a round-2 kept pool (326/350). The round-2 pool can only train an R3 adapter, which is never evaluated. Either a third adapter was trained and not reported, or the 163/175 figures are not optimizer steps behind any reported model. The steps relevant to the comparison are 220 and 196 (seed 1), giving 3.2–3.6× for no-filter and 0.8–0.9× for gold. These are consistent with '3–4×' and 'about the same', so the conclusion survives, but the listing invites the misreading that R2 reflects three rounds of training. Because of restart-from-base, the R2 model is one 196-step adapter trained on R1 outputs, not cumulative training. That should be stated wherever 'three rounds' or 'dose' is discussed (e.g. 'three evaluation points, two self-training iterations').

title: Scaling the 2.2-point bound to ~3 points contradicts the paper's own re-scored intervals
quote: 2.2-point bound on gains, which on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points
explanation: The paper takes the factor 0.73–0.78 (a ratio of point estimates in three declining runs: −8.3/−10.7 = 0.78, −4.7/−6.0 = 0.78, −2.4/−3.3 = 0.73) and applies it to 'every original-verifier difference and interval', so the 2.2-point upper bound becomes 2.2/0.75 ≈ 2.9. This would only hold if re-scoring multiplied every per-problem difference by one constant. The re-scored intervals the paper reports do not behave that way. Interval widths barely change: Run A 5e-4 seed 1 goes from [−12.3, −4.5] (width 7.8) to [−14.8, −6.7] (8.1); seed 2 from [−8.2, −1.2] (7.0) to [−9.7, −2.2] (7.5); 1e-5 seed 0 from [−4.8, 0.0] (4.8) to [−5.9, −0.7] (5.2). Widths grow by about 4–8%, not by the ~30% that dividing by 0.75 implies. Meanwhile the point estimates move further negative. The 2.2 bound comes from runs with negative point estimates (A at 1e-4, seeds 1 and 3: −1.5 [−5.3, 2.2] and −1.0 [−4.3, 2.2]). Applying the observed pattern (centre ×1.3, half-width ×1.05) to −1.5 [−5.3, 2.2] gives about −2.0 [−5.9, 2.0]: the upper end stays near 2, it does not move to 3. Rescaling an upper endpoint by a ratio of point estimates only makes sense for an interval centred on a positive gain. Neither run that sets the bound was re-scored. The '≈3 points' figure (also in the summary) is unsupported and probably wrong in direction. It should be dropped, or computed by actually re-scoring the runs that set the bound.

title: The 15.5–18.4% 'storage defect' share and r_t mix in the unparseable-gold defect, which cannot be adapted to by construction
quote: in \boxed{}, the re-score described below, makes 46 of these 51 golds parseable,
explanation: V′ wraps the gold in \boxed{}, and this also makes 46 of the 51 previously unparseable MATH-500 golds parseable. On those problems V rejects every sample, whatever its form, and V′ accepts the correct boxed ones. So every correct boxed generation on these ~46 problems (~9% of problems) lands in the numerator of r_t. The paper admits the overlap ('the two corrections overlap and should not be added'), but the abstract, §3.2 and §5.3 still call the 15.5–18.4% a single 'storage defect' and use its flatness as the adaptation test. The format probe suggests the unparseable part is large. Of the 41 boxed-probe rejections, 24 come from unparseable golds and only 17 (8.5%) are the compound/bare-gold class. The FN audit, which excludes unparseable golds, finds 7.8%. Together these suggest that roughly half of the 15.5–18.4% is the unparseable-gold component. That component cannot fall through adaptation: those problems never enter the pool, never give training signal, and no output form is accepted by V. Its share of r_t can move only through changes in relative accuracy on those problems. A flat r_t is therefore partly guaranteed by construction, which weakens 'the model does not adapt to this defect'. The same mixing affects the pool figure 440→542 used in check (iii) and in §3.2, since newly parseable selection-set problems add examples too. Fix: report r_t (and the pool enlargement) separately for (a) problems whose gold V parses and (b) the 46 newly parseable ones, and make (a) the adaptation test.

title: As instantiated, r_t is not a clean adaptation test: V′ depends on the prediction's format, no feasible V-accepted correct form is shown, and r_t moves with style and problem mix
quote: the gold in \boxed{} when the prediction contains one and the gold does not
explanation: The logic is 'r_t falls iff the model adapts to V'. Four things weaken it here. (1) V′ wraps the gold only when the prediction contains \boxed{}. For unboxed generations V′ = V, so they can never be in the numerator. So r_t ≈ (boxed share among V′-accepted) × P(V rejects | boxed, V′ accepts). A fall in boxed usage, which the paper reports and says it cannot attribute to imitation or drift, lowers r_t mechanically. The test then has the same imitation-vs-drift confound the paper cites for style counts. The reason for the conditional wrap, rather than always wrapping the gold, is not given. (2) Adaptation needs a correct form that V accepts. For a compound bare gold parsed to its first number, a correct boxed answer can never pass. The only accepted outputs are unboxed text parsed the same way, or a wrong answer equal to the first number. The paper does not show that a learnable, correct, V-accepted form exists, so 'r_t should fall' is not established as a prediction. (3) r_t is not controlled for composition. As accuracy falls, which problems contribute correct answers changes, and compound-answer problems may differ in difficulty. So r_t can drift without adaptation, or a fall can be masked. The 'direction-free' test is therefore not independent of accuracy changes. (4) The paper's own train-on-gold data show the defect share moving with output style and no verifier involved: 0.7/16.0 ≈ 4% at seed 1 and 3.3/13.3 ≈ 25% at seed 2, against ~17% at round 0. So a fall in r_t is not specific to adapting to V, and a flat r_t mainly says the boxed answer style did not change. With no interval on r_t and three runs, the paper's 'rules out strong adaptation' wording is about as far as the evidence goes. The abstract's unqualified 'the model does not adapt to this defect' goes further. A problem-fixed version (r_t on a fixed set of problems, boxed generations only) with a bootstrap interval would help.

title: The 0.73–0.78 'understatement factor' is a composite of two effects, is outside range for train-on-gold, and is extrapolated to every table
quote: understated (by a factor of about 0.73–0.78)
explanation: Arithmetic check: the three self-training ratios are 0.78, 0.78 and 0.73. Train-on-gold, re-scored in the same analysis, gives −19.7/−24.7 = 0.80 and −18.7/−22.0 = 0.85, both outside the stated range. A constant defect share f ≈ 17–20% of correct answers would predict a factor of 1−f ≈ 0.80–0.83. The lower observed 0.73–0.78 is consistent with a second effect: the always-zero unparseable-gold problems (11–18 per partition, ≈7–12%) add no change under V but do under V′. So the factor depends on how many dead problems a partition has and on accuracy changes on those problems; it is not a property of the verifier. Extending it to 'every original-verifier difference and interval', to runs never re-scored (all of 1e-4 and 2e-4, Run B, no-filter, Run C), to pass@k, and to the claim that all tables are '4.7–8.0 points too low' is unsupported. The 4.7–8.0 offsets are pass@1 on MATH-500 exams from five runs. GSM8K (0% audited FN, numeric golds) and Design P are presumably mostly unaffected, and pass@k offsets were not reported. The paper should state the factor's derivation and range (including train-on-gold), limit it to the re-scored runs, and restrict the 'too low' statement to MATH-500 pass@1.

title: False-positive rate left unmeasured, though the audit data permit an estimate and the defect itself implies false positives for both V and V′
quote: so it cannot measure the false-positive rate; that the verifier rarely accepts wrong
explanation: The FN audit scored all 176 parseable-gold MATH-500 solutions with a scripted correctness check: 128 correct, 48 not recognised as correct. The verifier's decision on those 48 is available, so at least an upper bound on the false-positive rate can be computed from data already in hand. 'Inspected only rejections' describes a choice of analysis; it does not mean FP is unmeasurable. FP matters for three claims. (a) The defect description implies a structural FP channel in V: if a bare compound gold such as 3\sqrt{13} is parsed to its first number, then a wrong prediction \boxed{3} matches it. The pool can therefore contain wrong 'accepted' answers on exactly the defect problems, and adapting to V there would mean writing such answers, which r_t (defined over V′-accepted generations) cannot see. (b) The 30-flip hand check found one flip with an empty box. That is an apparent false positive of V′ (~3% of flips), against the stated assumption that V′ accepts no wrong answer. (c) 'Correct' in every table means V-accepted, so FP inflates every pass rate. The paper should report the FP estimate from the audit data, check how often V accepts a prediction equal to the first number of a compound gold, and say what the empty-box case implies for V′.

title: FN audit: the 'wrong-token extraction' diagnosis is probably confounded with the gold-storage defect, and the 7.8% has a restricted denominator and no interval
quote: the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128) on MATH-500
explanation: §3.2 says 'most failures are wrong-token extraction from a long solution'. The basis for the label is that 8 of 10 cases are 'accepted when only the boxed answer is' verified. Appendix B says most of these 8 are compound answers (3\sqrt{13}, 6−5i, 11\sqrt{2}, ...) and overlap with the bare-gold class. This raises a confound the paper does not rule out. If the extracted answer is passed without its box delimiter, it may be parsed exactly as the bare gold is (to its first number), and then match by accident. On that reading, the 'boxed-only accepted' test would show the gold-storage defect, not a long-solution extraction failure. The paper hedges that 'the two labels describe where the failure shows', but the main text still states the extraction diagnosis, and it presents the gold-storage defect as a separate post hoc discovery the audit apparently already saw. Also: the denominator keeps only answers the authors' normaliser recognises as correct (128 of 176). Compound answers are where both the normaliser and math-verify are weakest, so FN on exactly the problematic class is probably understated. The audit uses Qwen2.5-7B solutions, not the loop's outputs. And a Wilson interval is given for GSM8K 0/200 but not for MATH-500 10/128, which is roughly [4.3%, 13.8%]. The authors should state exactly what string was passed in the 'boxed-only' check, give the interval, and reconcile 7.8% with the loop's 15.5–18.4%, most of the gap probably being the unparseable-gold overlap.

title: Unparseable golds 'cancel within a partition' only for level offsets in differences, not for relative effects, conditional metrics or cross-partition comparisons
quote: which lowers absolute pass rates but cancels
explanation: The 51 unparseable golds (11–18 per exam partition) add a constant zero in each round, so they cancel in a within-run difference of sample accuracy or pass rates. But: (1) they dilute every change by the share of dead problems, 7–12% depending on the partition. Comparisons of decline size across seeds/partitions (e.g. 'the decline may grow with the rate on one seed', seed 1 vs seed 2) therefore carry partition-dependent dilution, and level comparisons across partitions carry offsets up to ~5 points (18 vs 11 dead problems). (2) Conditional and ratio measures do not cancel: matched finished accuracy, the finished/cap-share decomposition and the 'Fin. share' of Table 7, and r_t all include these problems. Their generations count as finished-but-wrong or cap-hit, so a change in termination on these problems moves 'finished accuracy' even though their correctness cannot change. (3) Under V′ they become scorable (46/51), so the 'cancellation' is exactly what makes original and re-scored changes differ (see the factor issue). The paper should state the number of dead problems per partition, and preferably report the main metrics with these problems excluded.

title: Training limit of 512 tokens including the prompt, with a 512-new-token generation cap, means accepted examples are trained without their answer or EOS
quote: with a training sequence limit of 512 tokens
explanation: Any kept solution can be up to 512 generated tokens, but the training sequence (prompt + solution) is cut at 512. With standard right-truncation, every kept solution longer than 512 − (prompt length) loses its ending: the final \boxed answer and the end-of-turn/EOS token. The summary reports 24–26% of the pool truncated. Two consequences matter for the paper's claims. (a) For a quarter of the pool, the verifier filter does not actually decide what is trained on: the trained text no longer contains the verified answer, so these are not 'kept correct solutions' in the GVT sense. (b) Training on sequences that stop mid-solution without EOS directly teaches non-termination. That is a plausible mechanism for the cap-hit increases at 5e-4 that §4.5 decomposes, and a design-induced cause of decline rather than a property of self-training. The paper does test this partly (one 1024-limit run and one retrain without truncated examples, both at seed 1, reported 'within the noise of single runs'). But the main configuration has the flaw, no rationale is given for setting the limit equal to the generation cap, and the truncation side is not stated. It also matters that the 1024-limit run (−5.7) is closer to the same-configuration replicate (−5.2) than to the original (−8.3). The method should state truncation side and EOS handling, give the truncation rate per run, and either fix the limit or treat it as a named confound in the conclusions about decline.

title: Loss over the prompt is an unjustified, unablated design choice that interacts with duplicate problems and with the token budget
quote: learning-rate decay and no warmup; loss over the whole chat sequence, prompt
explanation: Computing loss on the prompt departs from standard rejection-sampling SFT (completion-only loss), and no reason is given. In this setup a problem can contribute up to k accepted solutions, so its statement and the fixed instruction are trained up to k times per round. At 5e-4 this adds a strong gradient signal unrelated to solving and invites memorising the problem text. It also uses part of the 512-token training budget, which worsens truncation of the solution. Because the paper attributes declines at high learning rates to self-training dynamics (less accurate finished solutions, more cap-hits), a training-objective choice that could itself cause degradation should be justified or ablated, or at least listed among the confounds. The paper should also state the per-round count of duplicate problems and whether samples were deduplicated.

title: Reproducibility gaps: what a 'seed' controls, where replicate nondeterminism comes from, shared round-0 generations, and the inference setup
quote: A “seed” sets the exam partition, the selection set and the training
explanation: A seed is said to fix the partition, the selection set and the training randomness. Yet a 'same-configuration' replicate (Run A, 5e-4, seed 1) ends 3.2 points away, and Runs A and B at seed 2 have identical round-0 pools (424) but end 7.3 points apart in pass@1. If training and sampling were fully seeded, identical pools would give identical round-1 adapters. So something is not controlled (fp16 GPU nondeterminism, unseeded or batch-dependent sampling, data-loader order). The paper never says what, although these replicate gaps are used to calibrate training-seed variance. Also unstated: whether round-0 generations are produced once and shared across runs with the same seed (Tables 4 and 6 show identical R0 values 33.3/50.0/33.7 across three rates, which suggests they are); the generation engine and batching/padding (HF generate vs vLLM, fp16); whether the chat template's default system prompt is included; whether multiple accepted samples of the same problem are deduplicated; truncation side; and how cap-hit was recorded (re-tokenising to ≥508 rather than using the generation's finish reason is an approximation and should be justified). These details decide whether the runs can be reproduced, and they bear directly on the paper's noise arguments.

title: All headline numbers are graded by a verifier known to reject ~1/6 of correct answers; 'the loop trained with it' does not justify using it as the evaluation measure
quote: “Correct” always means accepted by the verifier (preset reward), the
explanation: The same verifier V selects training data and grades the held-out exam. The paper then finds that V rejects 15.5–18.4% of V′-accepted generations, yet keeps V in every table, 'since that is the verifier the loop trained with'. That is a reason to use V for selection, not for measuring mathematical ability, which is the research question. For the 'no gain' claim, grading with V is partly conservative: adaptation to V would raise V-scores, so an absence of V-gains is informative. But for magnitudes (declines, finished-accuracy losses, the decomposition, the 2.2 bound), the better-calibrated grader should be primary, or both should be shown side by side. Re-scoring is cheap (saved generations, CPU-only), and only five runs were re-scored, so the conclusions that all other declines 'would also survive a re-score' rest on extrapolation from three. Re-scoring all runs with V′, plus an independent check (e.g. the scripted normaliser), would remove most of the factor/extrapolation issues above.

title: The illustrative example of the gold-storage defect is written backwards
quote: so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold (e.g. \frac43
explanation: The sentence describes a boxed prediction failing against a bare gold, but the example reads '\frac43 against \boxed{\frac{4}{3}}', which shows a bare form against a boxed one, apparently the other way round. It is also not clear which of \frac43 / \frac{4}{3} is the stored gold. Appendix B's mechanism ('the bare gold is parsed to its first number') makes this matter: for gold '\frac43' the first number would be 4, so a correct 4/3 would fail and a wrong '4' would pass. That is the false-positive channel raised in a separate comment. A precise example (stored gold string, prediction string, what each side parses to) would remove the ambiguity.

title: "Nor does it improve" turns absence of a detected gain into evidence of absence; the bound that would justify it is wider than 2.2 points
quote: Nor does it improve.
explanation: §5.1 and §I.1 phrase the result correctly as 'Not detectably', and App C itself says an interval that includes zero 'does not rule an effect out'. The abstract ('Nor does it improve') and the introduction ('Our answer is negative on the first branch') instead state a flat negative. The bound offered in support is weaker than its number suggests, for four reasons. (a) 2.2 is the largest per-run upper end in Table 5 (10^-4 seeds 1 and 3). Claiming that no run gains more than 2.2 is a joint statement over about 13 self-training runs, and its joint coverage is well below 97.5% (Bonferroni gives only >=67%). (b) It leaves out training-seed variance, which the paper estimates from a replicate pair at 3.2 points apart. Adding that variance in quadrature is rough arithmetic: bootstrap SE about 1.9 (from interval width / 3.92), plus a per-run seed SD of about 3.2/sqrt(2) ≈ 2.3, gives a combined SE of about 3.0. For a run like 10^-4 seed 1 (-1.5) the upper end then becomes about +4.4. (c) On the re-scored verifier scale, which the paper says shrinks every difference by 0.73–0.78, that is about +6. (d) There is no pre-set equivalence margin (J.10). With all this, the data are consistent with modest gains of 4–6 sample-accuracy points in individual runs. A pooled or random-effects estimate across runs and seeds would give a meaningful bound. Without one, the abstract and introduction should keep the 'not detectably' wording used in §5.1.

title: No power or minimum-detectable-effect analysis, so the reader cannot tell how informative the null is
quote: a single 150-problem pass@1 has a standard error of
explanation: The headline negative result rests on 150 held-out problems, but the paper never states which effect sizes its design could detect. From Table 5, paired pass@1 intervals are about ±6.7–7.5 points wide, pass@k about ±6, and sample accuracy about ±2.5–3.8. At 80% power and two-sided alpha 0.05, the minimum detectable effect is about 2.8 SE: roughly 9–10 points for pass@1, about 8 for pass@k, and about 4–5 for sample accuracy. That is before seed variance and before the 0.73–0.78 understatement factor. So the pre-set measures (pass@1, pass@k) could detect only large gains. The statement that 'no pass@1 or pass@k gain has an interval excluding zero' carries little information beyond the sign of the point estimates. Stated positively, the null is informative against gains of the size cited in the introduction from RLVR (tens of points), and much less so against the few-point gains typical of SFT self-training. Saying this would make the negative result more precise and more honest.

title: Abstract states post hoc results without the post hoc label the body attaches to them
quote: gains above 2.2 points, a loose bound that omits training-seed variance.
explanation: §3.4 says that claims resting on sample accuracy, 'including the 2.2-point bound, are therefore post hoc in the choice of measure'. §4.5 calls the finished-accuracy analysis 'post hoc and descriptive', and App H says the matched metric 'conditions on an outcome of training and is descriptive, not a causal effect'. The abstract qualifies the 2.2-point bound only for seed variance, not for the post hoc choice of measure or the lack of an equivalence margin. It also gives 'finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate' as a plain headline finding, with no mention that it comes from a post hoc, post-treatment-conditioned metric. That metric drops 22–45 problems per run and uses a baseline that App H admits is biased for 6–21 problems. The abstract does label the r_t test 'post hoc', so the labelling is inconsistent. The paper applies its own standard of marking post hoc analyses in the body but relaxes it exactly where readers look first.

title: Categorical claim of 'no adaptation' from a post hoc test with no interval, against the paper's own standard for single intervals
quote: the model does not adapt to this defect
explanation: App C warns that even a single interval excluding zero is not enough evidence, and J.10 asks for caution with intervals that only just exclude zero. The paper also faults its pre-set rule for being uninformative. Yet the strongest positive claim in the abstract and contributions, that the model 'does not adapt to this defect' (contributions: 'for that defect the model does not adapt'), rests on a post hoc statistic. That statistic has no interval, no trend test, no stated null, and no power analysis, and it covers three runs, two of them on the same configuration and rate. §5.3 itself limits the claim: 'it rules out strong adaptation to this defect, not weak adaptation'. Even that limit is not quantified, because 'strong' is never defined. The 15.5–18.4% band means r_t varies by about 3 points across rounds and runs, which would be a relative fall of up to about 16% within one run. The abstract should match the hedge in §5.3 and give, for example, a per-run slope with a problem-level bootstrap interval, plus the smallest fall the test could detect.

title: One of the three r_t runs is at a rate the paper says barely changes outputs: the same no-power flaw the paper criticises in the patch control
quote: in every round of the three runs we re-scored (Run A at 5×10−4, two seeds, and
explanation: The third r_t run is Run A at 10^-5. App E says this rate 'changes the outputs little' (length and cap-hit unchanged), and that a flat curve there 'is evidence that this training step did little'. A flat r_t at 10^-5 is therefore expected whether or not the loop would adapt to V. This is the same logic the paper uses to dismiss the \dfrac patch control ('Its null is expected whatever the truth', J.2). The two cases are judged by different standards. Effectively, the evidence for 'no adaptation' is the two 5×10^-4 runs on two partitions. In those runs the model is degrading overall (less accurate finished solutions, more cap-hits), so a failure to learn the accepted form is hard to separate from general degradation. The paper should count the 10^-5 run as uninformative and say that the claim rests on two runs.

title: r_t is not adjusted for the changing problem mix, although the paper applies matching to finished accuracy for exactly this reason
quote: If the model learns to write what V accepts, rt should fall over rounds, whatever
explanation: The gold-storage defect is triggered by how a problem's gold answer is stored, combined with the prediction's form. So whether a V'-accepted generation is rejected by V depends largely on which problems the model solves. As accuracy falls and the solved set changes (Table 4: 14–36 problems lost per run), r_t can stay flat while the per-problem rejected fraction falls, or the reverse. This is a composition effect. For finished accuracy the paper recognises this exact problem ('Because the problems that still finish change') and builds a matched metric. The r_t test, which supports the headline 'no adaptation' claim, gets no such treatment. A within-problem version (restricted to problems whose gold triggers the defect, weighted by a fixed problem mix), with a problem-clustered bootstrap, would apply the paper's own standard. Related point: the falling \boxed share (52%→36%) is a change in prediction form that interacts with a defect described as penalising \boxed answers. The paper should state the direction of that interaction for r_t.

title: Two different r_t-like statistics are reported for the same test, and the 10^-5 value (20%) falls outside the headline range
quote: round 0 and round 2 at seed 1 and 20% throughout at 10−5 (Appendix B). This
explanation: The abstract and §5.3 give r_t as 15.5–18.4% 'in every round' of three runs, including 10^-5. The same paragraph then gives a second figure, the defect's share of re-scored exam pass@1: 17% at seed 1 and '20% throughout at 10−5'. App B shows the 15.5–18.4% is computed over all 500 problems and all generations, while the 17%/20% is computed on the exam set's pass@1. The two have different denominators and different noise levels; pass@1 is a single draw on 150 problems. A reader cannot tell which is the test statistic, and 20% at 10^-5 sits outside the 15.5–18.4% band that the abstract says holds in every round of every run. The paper should define one statistic and report it per run and round, with an interval.

title: 'Five of six runs' counts near-replicates and runs that share a baseline as independent evidence
quote: vals excluding zero in five of six runs, while the cap-hit share rises 2–14 points.
explanation: The six 5×10^-4 MATH-500 runs (A, B, no-filter at seeds 1 and 2) come from only two exam partitions. Within a seed, all three share the same round-0 generations, so the matched baseline is shared, and A and B share almost all of their pool. §4.4 says correctly that 'same-seed A and B are closer to two replicates than four', and App E/I.1 make the same point for A and B at seed 0 at 10^-5. §4.5 and I.1 still report 'five of six' as if it were six independent confirmations; the same goes for the cap-hit statement 'in all three seed-2 runs'. Since seed sets the partition, these really amount to two partition-level observations with correlated intervals. Reporting them as 'both partitions' (with the per-seed pattern) would be consistent with the paper's own replicate accounting.

title: The cap-share split by seed is called 'qualitative' and possibly partition noise in App H, but is said to move the reading in §5.3
quote: the split moves the reading: at 5 × 10−4 the cap share accounts for 12–30% of
explanation: App H says the finished-accuracy shares 'have wide intervals' (e.g. 59% [−11, 114], 73% [43, 108]), that they split by seed, that 'this may be partition variation', and that 'What the table supports is qualitative'. §5.3(ii), the proposed audit protocol, and I.1 nonetheless present 12–30% versus 52–72% as a substantive finding that 'moves the reading'. These are ratios of two noisy differences, which are unstable when the total change is small (A, seed 2: −4.7), and the seed-1 and seed-2 intervals overlap. The ranges are point estimates over near-replicate runs (see the five-of-six comment). §5.3 should carry the App H caveat, or report the cap-share part in points with intervals rather than as a percentage of the decline.

title: Added/lost counts appear as supporting evidence in §5.1, although §3.4 says they are not an independent test
quote: the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained
explanation: §3.4 notes that added minus lost equals 150×Δpass@k, 'so these counts add only the gross churn behind the net change, not an independent test'. I.1 likewise says the count 'restates the sign of the pass@k change rather than adding evidence'. The main-text answer in §5.1 drops this qualifier and places the sentence right after the 2.2-point bound, as a further reason for 'Not detectably'. A reader of the main text alone would take it as extra evidence. It is the sign of Δpass@k, which Table 5 already reports with intervals, mostly including zero. title: Training-seed variance rests on a single replicate pair at a different rate, and the 'same size' comparison mixes a difference with an SD
quote: which is of the same size (a replicate of Run A at 5 × 10−4, seed 1, ends 3.2
explanation: The only direct estimate of training-seed variance is one replicate pair (Run A, 5×10^-4, seed 1). It gives a difference of 3.2 points, a variance estimate with one degree of freedom whose own uncertainty is very large. A difference between two runs has about sqrt(2) times the SD of a single run, so the implied per-run seed SD is about 2.3. The paper calls the 3.2 'of the same size' as the bootstrap half-widths, which compares a difference with a half-width. Also, the bound being questioned (2.2) comes from the 10^-4 and 10^-5 runs, where training changes outputs much less and seed variance could be smaller or larger; there is no replicate at those rates. The second illustration in App C (A vs B at seed 2, 7.3 points of pass@1) is a single-draw pass@1 contrast between arms that differ in treatment. The paper should say explicitly that seed variance is essentially unestimated at the rates behind the no-gain bound, rather than citing a precise-looking 3.2.

title: The 'about four of 76 by chance' heuristic is misapplied and used one-sidedly
quote: at the 95% level about four of the 76 would exclude zero by chance if nothing
explanation: The expected count of 76×0.05 ≈ 4 assumes the global null holds for all 76 intervals. Many are plainly non-null: train-on-gold (−18 to −26), Run C (−12 to −22), and most 5×10^-4 rows. The number of intervals for which 'nothing changed' is plausible is much smaller, so the expected count of false exclusions among them is lower, about 1–2 if roughly 30 are near-null. The count also includes the post hoc matched column, which uses a different re-scoring and 2,000 resamples. App E uses the heuristic to discount the 10^-5 seed-0 declines, but the multiplicity argument is not turned on the no-gain conclusion. There, the relevant issue is that the reported bound is the maximum of about 13 upper ends, so its joint coverage is below nominal. A family-wise or false-discovery-rate adjustment over a defined family (e.g. the 13 self-training Δsample-acc intervals), or a pooled analysis, would apply the multiplicity standard in both directions.

title: 'Fixed in advance' covers the measures only: the design itself (rates, k, rounds, controls) was adaptive, and no registration record is given
quote: Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little, we reran Run A at 10−4
explanation: The introduction says four measures and a reading rule were 'fixed in advance', which suggests pre-registration. No registration or timestamped protocol is cited. The learning-rate grid, the switch to k=4 and three rounds, the controls and the replicate were all chosen after seeing the 10^-5 results, and the primary measure, the cap-hit definition, the matched metric, the decomposition and the r_t test were all added afterwards. The paper is admirably open about most of these individually. Still, a headline such as 'no gain at four learning rates' comes from a sequence of data-dependent design choices, and Δpass@k mixes k=8 (10^-5) with k=4 (other rates). One sentence stating that only pass@1, pass@k, \boxed share and transitions plus the reading rule were pre-set, and that the rest of the design was adaptive, would prevent readers from crediting the study with more pre-specification than it had.
